record.field: Technique, training, gear and junior advice: practical notes from our coaches to help you play smarter.
Power comes from timing, not muscle. Break down the preparation, contact point and recovery that turn a good smash into a winning one.

The smash is badminton’s signature shot, but the hardest smashes rarely come from the strongest arms. They come from players who get behind the shuttle early, load their body correctly and strike at the highest possible point.

1. Get behind the shuttle

Every great smash starts with footwork. Move quickly to a position slightly behind where the shuttle will fall, side-on to the net, with your non-racket arm pointing up at the shuttle for balance and tracking.

2. Load from the ground up

Rotate your hips and shoulders away from the net and transfer weight onto your back leg. The power chain runs from legs to hips to trunk to shoulder, elbow and finally the wrist and fingers.

“Hit it high and in front. Angle beats speed every single time.”

3. Contact high and in front

Make contact at full stretch and slightly in front of your body. A higher contact point creates a steeper angle, which is far harder to defend than raw speed.

  • Relax your grip until the moment of impact, then squeeze.
  • Pronate the forearm through contact for a clean, flat strike.
  • Aim for the body or the tramlines, not the middle of the court.

4. Recover immediately

A smash is only as good as your next shot. Let your racket leg come through naturally and push back toward the centre, racket up, ready for the block return.
Five Footwork Drills Every Player Should Know
Fast feet win rallies. These five drills from our coaching team build speed, balance and efficient movement to all four corners.

Good footwork is invisible: it simply makes every shot feel easier. These five drills are staples of our Performance Training sessions. Do them two or three times a week and you’ll feel the difference within a month.

1. Six-corner shadow

Without a shuttle, move from the base to each of the six corners in a set order, mimicking a shot at each. Focus on a split step every time you return to centre.

2. Split-step reactions

A partner points to a random corner just as you land your split step. React, move, shadow the shot and recover. Ten reps, rest, repeat.

3. Lunge and recover

Practise deep forward lunges to the net with your racket leg leading, then push back explosively. Keep your chest up and your knee over your toes.

4. Chassé ladders

Side-to-side chassé steps along the back line build the quick, balanced movement you need to cover rear-court shots.

5. Multi-shuttle feeding

A coach or partner feeds shuttles rapidly to different areas. It combines everything above under real game pressure.

  • Warm up thoroughly before every footwork session.
  • Prioritise quality over speed until patterns feel natural.
  • Wear proper court shoes. Running shoes don’t grip the same way.
How to Choose the Right Badminton Racket
Weight, balance, flex and string tension explained, so you can pick a racket that suits your game rather than your favourite pro.

Walk into any pro shop and you’ll find dozens of rackets that look almost identical. The differences that matter come down to four things: weight, balance, shaft flexibility and string tension.

Weight

Racket weight is usually shown as a “U” rating. 3U (85–89g) and 4U (80–84g) suit most club players. Lighter rackets are faster to manoeuvre; heavier ones add stability and power.

Balance

Head-heavy rackets add momentum to smashes and clears. Head-light rackets are quick in defence and at the net. Even-balanced frames are a great all-round choice for developing players.

Shaft flexibility

Flexible shafts help generate power with a slower swing, ideal for beginners. Stiff shafts reward fast, well-timed swings with precision and control.

“Choose the racket for the player you are today, not the one you hope to be next year.”

String tension

Lower tensions (20–24 lbs) offer a bigger sweet spot and more forgiveness. Higher tensions give more control but demand cleaner contact.

  • Try before you buy: our rental rackets cover the main styles.
  • Ask a coach to watch you play and recommend a balance.
  • Restring regularly; old strings lose tension and feel.
Attack side-by-side, defend front-and-back, and never leave a hole. The simple rules behind smooth doubles rotation.

Most club doubles pairs lose points not because of bad shots, but because both players end up in the same place. Rotation is simply the habit of moving as a pair so the court is always covered.

The two basic formations

  • Attack (front and back): when your side is hitting down, one player smashes from the back while the partner covers the net.
  • Defence (side by side): when you lift, both players drop into a side-by-side position to cover the smash.

When to switch

The shot you play decides the formation. Hit down or play a tight net shot and you attack. Lift the shuttle and you defend. Say it out loud for the first few weeks, “attack” and “lift”, until it becomes instinct.

“Your shot decides your shape. Play down, go front-and-back. Play up, go side-by-side.”

Rotating after the smash

If the back player smashes straight, the front player moves across to cut off the straight block. If the smash goes cross-court, the front player shifts the other way. Always move towards where the reply is most likely to come.

Communication

Agree simple calls with your partner: “mine”, “yours”, “out”. Clear, early calls prevent clashes and stop the easy shuttle falling between you.
Ten minutes is all it takes to play better from the first rally and protect your knees, ankles and shoulders.

Badminton is explosive: sudden lunges, jumps and overhead swings. Going straight from the car park to smashing is the fastest way to a strained calf or a sore shoulder. This routine fits into ten minutes.

Minutes 1–3: raise the temperature

Light jogging around the court, side-steps, and skipping. You want to feel warm and slightly out of breath.

Minutes 4–6: mobilise

  • Arm circles forwards and backwards
  • Walking lunges with a twist
  • Ankle rolls and calf raises
  • Hip openers and leg swings

Minutes 7–8: move like a player

Shadow footwork to all four corners at half speed, then three-quarter speed. Add a split step each time you return to the centre.

Minutes 9–10: hit

Start with gentle clears and drives with your partner, then gradually build up. Save the full-power smashes until the end of the knock-up.

“The best players don’t skip the warm-up. They just make it look effortless.”
Rally points, 21-point games, serving sides and the 20-all rule: everything you need to keep score with confidence.

New players often worry more about the scoring than the shots. The good news: badminton scoring is simple once you know a few rules.

Rally-point scoring

Every rally wins a point, no matter who served. A game is played to 21 points, and a match is the best of three games.

The two-point rule

You must win by two clear points. At 20–20, play continues until one side leads by two, up to a maximum of 30. At 29–29, the next point wins.

Which side to serve from

  • Even score (0, 2, 4…): serve from the right service court.
  • Odd score (1, 3, 5…): serve from the left service court.
  • The server’s score decides the side, not the total.

Changing ends

Players change ends after each game, and in the third game when the leading side reaches 11 points.

“Even on the right, odd on the left. Learn that and you’ve learned half the rulebook.”
How to Prepare for Your First Tournament
From entering the right draw to managing nerves between matches: a practical checklist for tournament day.

Your first tournament is exciting and a little nerve-racking. Good preparation means you can focus on playing, not worrying about logistics.

The week before

  • Enter a draw that matches your level. A close match teaches more than a one-sided one.
  • Play match practice rather than just drills.
  • Restring your racket a few days before, not the night before.
  • Prioritise sleep in the last two nights.

What to pack

Two rackets, spare grips, two sets of kit, court shoes, water, snacks you know agree with you, a towel and a warm layer for between matches.

Between matches

Keep warm, sip water steadily and eat little and often. Watch your next opponent if you can and note their favourite shots and weaker side.

“Play the shuttle, not the scoreboard. One rally at a time.”

Afterwards

Write down three things that went well and one thing to work on. Bring that list to your next coaching session.
Why the Right Court Shoes Matter
Running shoes are built for straight lines. Badminton is all lunges and sudden changes of direction. Here’s what to look for.

Of all your kit, shoes have the biggest effect on both performance and injury risk. Running shoes are designed for forward motion, with soft, high heels that can roll on sideways movements.

What to look for

  • Gum rubber soles for grip on indoor courts without marking the floor.
  • Low profile to keep you close to the ground and stable when you change direction.
  • Lateral support around the forefoot for side-to-side movement.
  • Heel cushioning to absorb the impact of lunges.

Getting the fit right

Try shoes on with your playing socks, later in the day when feet are slightly larger. You want a snug heel and a thumb’s width of space at the toe.

When to replace them

If the sole is smooth in the forefoot or you start slipping, it’s time. For regular players that’s usually every 6–12 months.
The right age to start, what equipment to buy and how to keep young players enjoying the game for years.

Badminton is one of the best first racket sports for children: the shuttle is slow enough to hit, the court is small and rallies come quickly. Here’s how to give them a great start.

When to start

Children as young as five can enjoy badminton with mini rackets and slower shuttles. Structured coaching usually works best from around seven or eight.

Equipment

  • A junior racket that is shorter and lighter
  • Nylon shuttles for durability while learning
  • Proper indoor court shoes

Keep it fun

Young players stay with sports they enjoy. Games, challenges and playing with friends matter more than perfect technique in the early years.

“If they leave the court smiling and asking when they can come back, the session was a success.”

Next steps

Once they can rally and serve, a regular junior class builds skills, confidence and friendships, and opens the door to junior tournaments.
